title: Don't benchmark against outliers: judge your startup on your own trade-offs
summary: Jason Cohen argues that comparing your startup to Instagram, WhatsApp or Slack, or even to averages, breeds needless depression and bad decisions. The better question is what the best move is for your own company given your specific challenges, and whether a metric change is the right trade for you, your customers and your employees.

principles.text: Don't measure yourself against rarefied outlier companies; the yardstick of extremes is meaningless for your situation.
principles.quote: You mustn't judge yourself with the yardstick of other companies, particularly not against the rarefied few who dwell in the extremities of reality.

principles.text: Average or median benchmarks are no better: another company can be worse on a metric yet very successful for other reasons.
principles.quote: For every such condition, I can show you another company in an even worse condition with regard to that metric, but which is extremely successful because of other reasons.

principles.text: Ask what's best for your company given the specific challenges and benefits in front of you, not how you rank.
principles.quote: The right thing to ask is: "What is the best thing I can do for my company, with the specific challenges and benefits that I have in front of me?"

principles.text: For any metric, ask whether you're happy with it and whether changing it is the right trade against other metrics, innovation, lifestyle, and the people involved.
principles.quote: "Am I happy with this metric, and if I change it at the expense of other metrics, or of innovation, or of my lifestyle, or of my happiness, is that the right trade for me, for the company, for my customers, and for my employees?"

principles.text: If you can't reason about your own situation confidently, you'll compare your worst fears to others' public façades, which leads to bad answers.
principles.quote: If you're not confident in reasoning about yourself, you have no choice but to compare your worst fears (exaggerated negative) with the public façade of other people (exaggerated positive)
